title: Grid Illumination
statement:
An `n x n` grid has room for one lamp in every cell, and all lamps start switched off. Each pair `[row, col]` in `lamps` switches on the lamp in that cell; a cell that appears several times still holds just one lit lamp. A lit lamp lights its own cell and every cell that shares its row, its column, or either of its two diagonals.

Handle `queries` in order. For a query `[row, col]`, record `1` if at least one lit lamp currently lights that cell and `0` otherwise. Then switch off every lit lamp in that cell or in any of the (up to 8) cells touching it by an edge or a corner. Return the recorded values, one per query, in query order.
constraints: Every row and column index in lamps and queries is between 0 and n - 1
signature: int[] gridIllumination(int n, int[][] lamps, int[][] queries)
notes:
## Intuition

Asking every lamp whether it lights the query cell costs O(lamps) per query, far too slow for 20,000 of each. A lamp only matters through four lines: its row, its column, its diagonal (cells where `row - col` is the same) and its anti-diagonal (cells where `row + col` is the same). So keep a count of lit lamps on each line. A cell is lit exactly when one of its four lines has a positive count, and switching a lamp off just lowers four counts.

## Approach

1. Keep four maps from line id to lamp count: `rows`, `cols`, `diagonals` (keyed by `row - col`) and `antiDiagonals` (keyed by `row + col`).
2. Keep `lampsOn`, a set of `"row,col"` strings, so a repeated lamp is counted only once.
3. For each new lamp, add it to `lampsOn` and raise its four line counts with `change(row, col, 1)`.
4. For each query, the cell is `lit` if any of its four counts is positive; push `1` or `0`.
5. Visit the 3 x 3 block around the query. Every lamp found in `lampsOn` is removed and its four counts drop with `change(r, c, -1)`. Cells outside the grid are never in the set, so no bounds check is needed.

## Example 1, step by step

Lamps `(0,0)` and `(4,4)` both sit on diagonal `0`, so `diagonals` holds `0 → 2`; rows 0 and 4, columns 0 and 4 and anti-diagonals 0 and 8 each hold 1. Query `(1,1)`: its diagonal `1 - 1 = 0` has count 2, so it is lit, push `1`. The block around it contains `(0,0)`, which is switched off; `diagonals` drops to `0 → 1`. Query `(1,0)`: row 1, column 0 (now 0), diagonal 1 and anti-diagonal 1 are all empty, so push `0`. Answer `[1, 0]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(L + Q): each lamp is added once and each query does four lookups plus nine set checks.
- Space: O(L) for the set and the four maps.

## Pitfalls

- Duplicate lamps: counting `(2,2)` twice leaves its lines lit after it is switched off once.
- `row * n + col` overflows safe integers when `n` is 10^9, so the key is a string.
- The query cell itself is part of the block and must be switched off too.
- Only lamps that are still on may lower the counts; `lampsOn.delete` returns `false` for the rest.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rows`, `cols` | lit lamps per row and per column |
| `diagonals`, `antiDiagonals` | lit lamps per `row - col` and per `row + col` |
| `lampsOn` | the cells whose lamp is still on |
| `change` | adds `delta` to a lamp's four line counts |
| `lit` | whether the query cell is lit |
| `r`, `c` | a cell in the 3 x 3 block around the query |
| `answer` | the recorded 1s and 0s |
